entries.title: Lonnie Bunch Protected the Smithsonian From More Than Trump
entries.summary: As pressures bore down on an American institution, its secretary held firm.
entries.content:
As pressures bore down on an American institution, its secretary held firm.

Americans may not realize for many years just how lucky they were that Lonnie G. Bunch III led the Smithsonian Institution from 2019 to 2026. Bunch has announced that he will step down at the end of this year. He insists that the timing is his own, and we should do him the honor of believing him—notwithstanding the immense pressure the administration has applied to the Smithsonian generally and Bunch personally since Donald Trump returned to office last year.

Bunch, 73, would likely have chosen to retire earlier if not for his sense of duty—his conviction (which few dispute) that he was the best person to guide the Smithsonian through a turbulent period. The Smithsonian is the world’s largest museum, education, and research complex. It’s also “part of the glue,” as Bunch himself said shortly after taking office, “that holds the country together.”

Since his appointment as the Smithsonian’s top official—its 14th secretary and the first historian and Black man to hold the position—in June 2019, Bunch has been the glue holding the Smithsonian together. Through a combination of principled stances and deft political skills, he has kept the sprawling institution on mission and aligned with its public. Chief Justice John Roberts, who serves as the Smithsonian’s chancellor, said in a statement that Bunch has “pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story” and that the Smithsonian has “benefited greatly from his wisdom, vision, and leadership.”

Bunch is a fighter, but a smart one. He has often struck me as a master of institutional jiu-jitsu—a leader who knows instinctively when to hold the line, when to yield, and how to convert yielding to the advantage of the institution he has done so much to advance and protect. “When you’re Black in America,” he told The New York Times earlier this year, “you’ve got to figure out how to get through, right? You’ve got to figure out how to build allies, when to stand firm, when to bang the table. So in some ways, all of that prepared me for this moment.”

Bunch has worked at the Smithsonian since 1978, interrupted by stints at the California African American Museum in the 1980s and the Chicago Historical Society in the early 2000s. His tenure as secretary included the upheavals of 2020 and 2021, when—after the killing of George Floyd and amid the coronavirus pandemic—activists on the left were accusing museums across the country, including the Smithsonian, of being bastions of white privilege, colonialism, and cultural theft. Bunch remained calm and compassionate in the face of these critiques, compromising when appropriate, but never giving in to bullying.

It surely helped that his greatest achievement prior to becoming the Smithsonian’s top official was planning, raising funds for, and launching the National Museum of African American History and Culture. The museum, which opened to great fanfare in 2016, has been hugely popular. Under Bunch’s leadership, the museum balanced a forthright, profoundly moving description of slavery and its long aftereffects with exhibits that bear witness to the extraordinary flowering of African American culture, celebrating a panoply of achievements by Black Americans across many fields of human endeavor.

The Smithsonian was founded by an act of Congress in 1846. During the Civil War, it created a controversy by refusing to host a lecture series presented by abolitionists. The institution’s leadership eventually relented, but Frederick Douglass, the most prominent abolitionist of the day, was still not permitted to speak. At the 2019 ceremony installing him as secretary, Bunch referred back to those days: “Today we are here speaking in a place as an African American, where Frederick Douglass could not speak, but we are a different institution.”

Bunch’s leadership, and the Smithsonian’s resilience, has been severely tested since Trump’s return to power. Efforts by the institution to tell what Kim Sajet, the former director of the National Portrait Gallery, described as “a fuller, more American story” and “one that fosters connection, reflection and understanding” came into conflict with White House officials who felt that the “fuller story” being told was overly focused on moral failure, hypocrisy, and oppression.

The new administration was quick to target the Smithsonian. Some of what gave Bunch moral authority during the Biden years now threatened to work against him.

In March 2025, an executive order noted that the United States had witnessed “a concerted and widespread effort to rewrite our Nation’s history.” The Smithsonian, it stated, had, “in recent years, come under the influence of a divisive, race-centered ideology.” Trump announced that he was firing Sajet. The Smithsonian regents asserted that only Bunch had authority over such personnel decisions, but she resigned anyway.

More recently, the administration has ramped up pressure on the Smithsonian, demanding an overhaul of its presentations to rid them of perceived liberal bias and attempting to force its hand with explicit threats, such as pulling funding and erecting warning signs in front of the National Museum of American History. (Although it is independent, the biggest share of the institution’s budget comes from the federal government.)

Bunch has had to figure out how to handle these various assaults without allowing the Smithsonian’s mission to be compromised. He has said plenty on the public record—all of it sage and diplomatic, yet consistently firm on questions of principle. I can only imagine what private conversations he has been having on a daily basis.

Thanks to the double whammy of COVID and activist pressures, few leaders of any prominent organization have had a fun time since 2020. But Bunch has been the leader of an enormous—and enormously important—institution that’s explicitly in the business of (among other things) telling the American story at a time when the question of how to tell that story has become so fraught and divisive.

What to do in such circumstances? Perhaps Americans could all begin by just agreeing that the pandas in the National Zoo (which is part of the Smithsonian) are very, very cute. And then, perhaps, that the Apollo 11 command module in the National Air and Space Museum—the one that carried Neil Armstrong, Michael Collins, and Buzz Aldrin to the moon and back—is really cool. If so, perhaps they can next agree that Bunch, during his tenure at the helm of the Smithsonian, has been the exact combination of resolute leader and compassionate and good-humored public servant that America needed him to be.

entries.title: A Great Novel Becomes a Bad Show
entries.summary: Don’t watch The Shards. Go read the book instead.
entries.content:
For many readers, the career of the novelist Bret Easton Ellis is the standard for mainstream literary stardom. The biopic writes itself: While still a college undergraduate, Ellis strikes it big with his debut novel, 1985’s Less Than Zero, an unsentimental stenography of disaffected, privileged young adults in swanky Los Angeles. It’s soon adapted into a movie starring Robert Downey Jr. and James Spader, which itself bears little resemblance to the book. Nevertheless, Ellis’s renown skyrockets. By the time he turns 30, he’s seemingly done it all: published multiple best sellers (American Psycho, The Rules of Attraction) filled with materialistic ennui, cheap sex, and lurid death; been mythologized as part of a literary “Brat Pack” alongside writers including Jay McInerney and Tama Janowitz; rubbed elbows with celebrities of the music and film worlds; made lots of money (for a writer, at least); and become addicted to drugs.

Regardless of how you felt about his work—and readers had all sorts of opinions—his success couldn’t be denied. “If you were not a supporter of the Brat Pack, you simply had to accept us anyway,” he writes in his 2005 novel, Lunar Park, which is narrated by a semifictional version of himself. Such white-hot notoriety was rare in his time, and it’s rarer now. While a book can become a hit in many ways, you’re only young once—and though we’ve all been told about the virtues of writers who labor away unappreciated until they finally get their moment, it’s hard not to be a little envious of the ones who’re able to enjoy their spoils before knee pain sets in. It didn’t matter that, when I finally read Less Than Zero after college, I thought it was a relic best left in its era—the work of a poser trying too hard to convince readers of his secret depth. Ellis’s early works felt too significant, too settled, for me to really say much about; disputing him would have been like arguing with a redwood tree.

His reputation as a hedonistic provocateur made the release of his 2023 novel, The Shards, somewhat of a surprise, at least to me. On its face, The Shards is an autofictional murder mystery starring a teenage version of Ellis who, at the start of his senior year of high school, suspects that a new classmate is responsible for a series of gory killings around the school’s ritzy Sherman Oaks neighborhood. Novel-Ellis is working on an early draft of Less Than Zero, drawing from his own party-heavy lifestyle. The sensationalistic violence and substance-fueled navel-gazing—all of that sounds like a typical Ellis novel. Yet The Shards is not celebratory or defiant. It’s narrated by a much older Ellis, who looks back on his youth with regret and shame—about his closeted homosexuality, about his formative and long-dead teenage friendships—and rips apart his own mythos from the inside.

Parts of The Shards read like they could have used a more punitive editor—it’s a little long, and Ellis describes himself as “keyed-up” a few too many times. Yet the book’s hefty length—594 pages in hardcover—is conducive to novel-Ellis’s obsessiveness as he combs through memories for hidden meaning and tries to identify each emotion he felt during this chaotic time period. “The facts from that fall were receding from memory but being seventeen actually became clearer to me emotionally,” he writes. “I realized I had needed this distance of forty years to finally begin writing the book.” Now, he suggests, he can admit that Less Than Zero was indeed an act of mimicry—that he’d copied that book’s numbed affectation from a classmate. The cynicism of his early work had put me off, but here he seemed weary enough to let down his guard and, perhaps, tell a version of the truth.

The Shards has now been adapted for FX by Ryan Murphy, whose campy and provocative shows (Glee, American Horror Story, Feud) have helped define TV in the 21st century. In many ways, it’s a natural match. Murphy’s eye is consistently drawn to beauty, and to the machinations and aspirations of the rich. And though his scripts can be plenty outlandish, he knows when a performer should play it straight.

The early episodes seem to preserve much of Ellis’s plot. We begin by meeting Bret (played by Igby Rigney), an aspiring novelist and senior at the prestigious Buckley School in Sherman Oaks. Bret has recently started dating Debbie (Hayes Warner), a bottle-blond socialite; along with another couple, Susan (Kaia Gerber) and Thom (Graham Campbell), they constitute a glamorous foursome. Beneath this picturesque front is a more complicated reality. Susan and Thom may look like the perfect prom queen and king, but she’s grown restless in their relationship. And while Bret is quietly in love with Susan, he’s also been hooking up with some of his male classmates and wondering how to take advantage of the fact that Debbie’s father, Terry (Wes Bentley), a well-connected (and seemingly gay) movie producer, appears interested in giving him his big break.

These delicate dynamics are unsettled by the appearance of a mysterious new transfer student, Robert (Homer Gere), who looks like he walked right out of an Armani advertisement. Bret is transfixed by his new classmate and is convinced that he’s seen Robert before, at the movies, where he made an indelible impression. But Robert becomes strangely defensive about the encounter, and insists that Bret must have made a mistake. His denials and secretive behavior lead Bret to suspect that Robert is connected to the Trawler, a yet-unidentified serial killer who’s been targeting local teenagers. Bret’s obsession with proving his guilt slowly spins out of control.

Gruesome deaths, a pulsing ’80s soundtrack, dramatic conversations about people’s hidden motivations—it should be fun, and it sometimes is. As Robert, Gere conveys an alluring darkness; you can’t take your eyes off him, and neither can the show’s characters. Gerber’s Susan is beautifully nonchalant, a quality that propels her into Robert’s arms. (Gere and Gerber are the respective children of Richard Gere and Cindy Crawford, who used to be married.) And Jordan Roth is ridiculous but memorable as Steven, Terry’s assistant, who seems to be manipulating everyone behind the scenes.

Yet Murphy makes a subtle tweak that changes The Shards completely. The novel is told from the first-person perspective, which allows an older Bret to constantly remark on the described action with the benefit of time and perspective. Here, that framing device is snipped entirely. Bret still narrates, but voiceover-Bret is not Bret Easton Ellis, the middle-aged author of American Psycho who’s now looking backwards. It’s just Rigney, who plays young Bret, speaking from a vague near future, and sometimes obnoxiously. “Kids today have it fucking easy,” he sneers, which is new writing.

The elision of this metafictional narration is paired with a lot of new plot. Ellis co-wrote the first two episodes before being sidelined in a reported power struggle. (He has not promoted the show on his personal Instagram, nor did he appear at a glitzy launch party in July.) The other episodes depart drastically from the book’s structure. Murphy tacks on stray storylines: a dance competition on an American Bandstand–type local TV show, for instance, and a kidnapping plot involving a foulmouthed classmate who has what seems to be a form of Tourette’s. One episode has the characters monologuing at one another in Shakespearean verse while dressed in costume. The add-ons are tonally confusing and parceled out inconsistently. Some moments are played for show-stopping drama, only to be immediately abandoned. Other confrontations have the taste of corny reality TV, and the ’80s references are often played for laughs.

A blunter way of saying this: The new stuff is awful, and a waste of time. The show expands Bret’s outer world at the cost of his inner life (and screen time, as Rigney disappears for long stretches), but that outer world isn’t very interesting. The novel’s emotions have been strip-mined, leaving only the surface tensions of vain teenagers. Many TV adaptations of literature miss the mark, because the visual medium isn’t always well suited to novelistic storytelling, which can be both wide-angled and highly internal. But this misfire bears a particular irony. Since Less Than Zero, Ellis has been trailed by critics saying his work is shallow and trades in shock value. The Shards show unfurls as if all of those put-downs were true, as though the book is little more than a collection of unsettling murders, great outfits, and hot people being mean to one another.

Two comments about the making of the show—both from that launch party—reveal something about what went awry. The first comes from Murphy, speaking about what drew him to the book: “I knew the songs, I knew the clothes, I knew everything because I had lived it. It was my time.” The second is from Roth, speculating on the show bringing about a trend revival: “Love Story got us our ’90s nostalgia, and Shards brings us our ’80s nostalgia.”

The former comment is Murphy viewing The Shards as his story, not Ellis’s—a tricky approach for a book that’s so explicitly personal. The latter is, I think, deeply cynical about the point of a show like this. Even when The Shards invites us to laugh at its characters, it does so through the prism of “Weren’t the ’80s crazy?” The emotions are blustery, but not intimate; the narration has been edited for cool concision. In the book, novel-Ellis narrates about Robert: “The boy aroused something primal in me that I had never felt before—I wanted him immediately, I needed to be his friend, I had to make contact, I had to see him naked, I had to own him.” In the show, this confessional surge has been drastically pared back, keeping Bret’s messy feelings at a distance.

Regret and shame, the novel’s animating sentiments, are not sexy; I’m sure the actors had more fun overindexing on the ’80s of it all. The end result, though, is the transformation of a great novel into a bad show, one that Murphy wants to run for two more seasons. Let’s hope not. Although Ellis is often nitpicky about adaptations of his work—he’s never come around to the wonderfully caustic movie version of American Psycho—he’s right to distance himself from this one. “It was nothing like the book,” Bret narrates in both the show and the novel, after coming out of a screening of The Shining. “I felt cheated.” It’s quietly tragic that the same thing has happened here.

entries.title: The Sadness of Being the ‘Last Man’
entries.summary: Francis Fukuyama has long been considered a naive triumphalist. He now wants to set the record straight.
entries.content:
Francis Fukuyama has long been considered a naive triumphalist. He now wants to set the record straight.

Francis Fukuyama never promised us we’d be happy.

To be fair to the many readers who thought otherwise, The End of History and the Last Man, his famous 1992 book, did give off a whiff of utopia, trumpeting a post–Cold War world in which liberal democracy had vanquished competing political systems and everyone could lie back on their affordable chaise longues and raise a glass to the expiration of all strife and struggle. “Several” people each week still ask the poor man whether he would like to unwrite that book, he says. Yet Fukuyama insists today that if you had read to the last page—in fact, the last five chapters—you would not have expected serenity. His more sober forecast is right there in the original essay that led to the book: “The end of history will be a very sad time.”

Fukuyama has published a new memoir, In the Realm of the Last Man, in which he hopes to shake off a reputation that he clearly can’t stand. He is not a naive Pollyanna, and he never was. By the “end of history,” he did mean that we had arrived at the best of all possible worlds—and he still does. But being the “Last Man,” inhabiting this ending, was always presented as an unstable condition. Fukuyama borrowed the concept from the dark mind of Friedrich Nietzsche, who used it to refer to a person bored out of their senses, someone who lives in a society where there is nothing left to risk their life for.

What appeared in his earlier book as an alarming afterthought is now front and center for Fukuyama. He wrote The End of History during a time of American triumphalism, as the Berlin Wall was turned into rubble, but the events of the past three decades—9/11, the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, Donald Trump—have offered up a different story. Fukuyama knows this. His defensiveness keeps him from fully acknowledging how far he’s had to step back from his own previously boosterish views, but he speaks about liberal democracy, this supposedly happy end state, in much gloomier tones. It now sounds like a scary cul-de-sac at night, where the streetlight is busted, an eerie tension fills the air, and there seems to be no way forward.

Purely as a memoir, I should say, this one is disappointing. Fukuyama loses interest in telling his own life story around page 60. The fun and revealing anecdotes are front-loaded. For example, as a young foreign-policy analyst, he kept failing a CIA polygraph test because a question about whether he had ever had sex with a man got him completely flustered (he hadn’t, he hastens to tell us). He writes about his father, a sociologist and committed liberal, who never stopped giving Fukuyama a hard time for his once-conservative political opinions (he did work for Ronald Reagan and the RAND Corporation, after all), telling him he was “brainwashed” by other people. When these more intimate insights taper off, so does any causal connection between Fukuyama’s personal background and his evolving thinking. His grandparents were Japanese immigrants who spent World War II in an internment camp. But this is only briefly mentioned, which left me wondering whether the stories they told him made him more attuned to the vulnerabilities of a pluralistic society.

We do get a few chapters about what an unapologetic gearhead he is, a lover of woodworking who can also assemble a computer from scratch. Yet Fukuyama spends most of his time and energy on summarizing the ideas that have animated his work, producing a greatest-hits album of insights. This succession of shifting concepts helps clarify how much the bravado that marked The End of History has seeped out of his work. The invasion of Iraq and the long chaos that followed were a turning point. Fukuyama broke with the neocon friends and mentors who had shaped his career until then. His first published piece of writing, in 1979, had been in Norman Podhoretz’s Commentary magazine, and he had once revered the Iraq War architect Paul Wolfowitz as “one of the smartest people I had ever met.” But after that war was launched, in 2003, he stopped speaking with them. He even found himself taking a particularly awkward silent elevator ride with the conservative columnist Charles Krauthammer.

By the late 2000s, Fukuyama was referring to himself as a “realistic Wilsonian.” He is still idealistic about democracy, but he sees that democracy alone is not some kind of fairy dust that can be sprinkled on randomly chosen countries; it is meaningless without institutions and a strong state to ensure the rule of law. His work from over the past two decades has supported this point—especially his two-book Political Order series. “Creating a modern, effective state was a much more difficult task than creating a democracy,” he writes in the memoir, looking back at America’s dead ends in Iraq and Afghanistan. Among the unsexy chapters are those in which he extols the value of an impersonal bureaucracy as crucial for a well-functioning polity, as opposed to one in which a leader hands out jobs to cronies and personally enriches himself.

Liberal democracy will not be dethroned, Fukuyama insists—mostly because no one has come up with a better idea. In response to the global rise of anti-liberal movements, many people across the political spectrum have blamed liberalism itself, casting it as a dilapidated system that should be torn down to the studs. But as far as Fukuyama is concerned, every alternative vision has either already been discredited or would lead to a worse world. The ultimate value of liberalism, he argues, is that it delivers on a fundamental human need better than any other framework (though it could still use plenty of tweaking).

We are defined, he explains, by thymos, a drive for recognition. Almost as much as we need food to live, we demand to have our worth acknowledged. We want respect. And this can be fully realized only in a liberal society where all people have equality under the law. Although “stuff”—Fukuyama’s word—might still happen, since the late 18th century, an increasing number of people have lived with a political system that has at least the potential to scratch everyone’s thymos. And this is why we have reached the end. Full stop.

But there is a problem: It’s really dull here. As much as we desire the autonomy and dignity that come with recognition, we are also drawn to the risk and struggle that were involved in achieving that recognition in the first place. Just because liberal democracies now satisfy the thymotic urge, this doesn’t mean that humans don’t still want something to die for. As Fukuyama explains it in the memoir, “the peace and prosperity brought about by a liberal order based on equal recognition is not enough for many people. They do not want to be recognized as the equals of every other person on earth.” Our horizons have been “flattened,” and it has made us restless and angry.

This is sad. It is depressing to think that we are incapable of just enjoying the fruits of liberal democracy, and of doing the incremental renovation work of making it function even better for the largest number of people. Instead we “struggle for the sake of struggle,” as Fukuyama put it in his original essay, because we “cannot imagine living in a world without struggle.” Eventually, this means turning on liberal democracy itself—inventing conspiracy theories to stoke our fury, valorizing strongmen, idealizing deadly premodern practices and values—which is how Fukuyama understands the populist and antidemocratic rebellions of the past decade.

All of this might sound cynical if it didn’t have some serious explanatory value. Take his critique of pro-Palestinian protests on college campuses. Without ignoring the very real death and destruction in Gaza, Fukuyama says these students are basically bored: “What they want is a break from their lives of steady but unheroic striving to get into those universities, and to experience danger and risk in pursuit of a just cause that has never previously been a major part of their lives. No more than the MAGA right do they have a clear vision of what type of future society they want to live in.” We have plenty of energy for tearing things down, he thinks, but liberal democracy is a logic problem that has already been solved, and it cannot be unsolved or reconfigured.

Fukuyama wants to be able to say I told you so. And on these grounds, his book does remind us that he did. But there is little comfort in this. What he has identified is a human problem: the blink of an eye that separates utopia from dystopia. We got what we always wanted, but it is not enough and never will be. “We have means of distributing resources a bit more evenly and should undertake to do that,” Fukuyama, the ever lucid analyst, writes. “What we lack is a way of distributing respect.” That desire for recognition won’t be sated, and this fact is the most dangerous thing for all of us.
